benefits_en:
1. Fasting is a protective shield (Junnah) guarding against sin in this world and Hellfire in the Hereafter.
2. When provoked, the fasting person responds with dignity: 'Indeed, I am fasting.'

1. Whoever fasts Ramadan with sincere faith and anticipation of Allah's reward will have all their past sins forgiven.
2. Ramadan is a supreme annual station for spiritual renewal and forgiveness.

1. Whoever stands in prayer during the nights of Ramadan (Tarawih/Qiyam) with faith and anticipation will have all past sins forgiven.
2. Night vigils illuminate the heart and purify the soul.

1. Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr) with faith and anticipation will have all past sins forgiven.
2. Laylat al-Qadr is superior in value to a thousand months of worship.

1. The breath of the fasting person is more pleasant to Allah than the scent of musk.
2. Allah uniquely attributes fasting to Himself: 'Fasting is for Me, and I shall reward it.'

1. In Paradise there is a gate called Ar-Rayyan, reserved exclusively for the fasting people; none other will enter through it.
2. Special divine honor and eternal refreshment for fasting believers.

1. The fasting person experiences two great joys: joy upon breaking the fast, and supreme joy upon meeting their Lord.
2. Earthly fulfillment leads directly to eternal delight in the Divine Presence.

1. When Ramadan arrives, the gates of Paradise are opened wide, the gates of Hellfire are shut, and the devils are chained.
2. An atmosphere of divine grace, mercy, and heightened inclination toward good deeds.

1. The blessing of the pre-dawn meal (Suhoor): 'Take Suhoor, for indeed in Suhoor there is blessing (Barakah).'
2. Provides physical vitality and follows the prophetic practice.

1. Hastening to break the fast (Iftar) as soon as the sun sets brings continuous goodness to the Muslim community.
2. Adherence to prophetic practice and avoiding religious excess.

1. Breaking the fast on fresh ripe dates (Rutab), dry dates (Tamr), or water before praying Maghrib.
2. Wholesome nutritional guidance and gentle revival of the body.

1. Whoever provides food for a fasting person to break their fast receives a reward equal to theirs, without reducing the faster's reward.
2. Multiplying rewards through hospitality and community support.

1. True fasting requires abandoning falsehood: whoever does not abandon false speech and malicious action, Allah has no need for their fasting.
2. Fasting must encompass the tongue, eyes, ears, and conduct.

1. When insulted or disputed with while fasting, compose yourself and say: 'Inni Sa'im' (I am fasting).
2. Emotional discipline and de-escalation under provocation.

1. Whoever eats or drinks out of genuine forgetfulness while fasting should complete their fast, for Allah has fed them and given them drink.
2. Divine mercy and absence of sin for unintentional mistakes.

1. Seeking the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr) in the odd-numbered nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan.
2. Intensifying worship, night prayer, and seclusion in the mosque (I'tikaf).

1. The comprehensive du'a for Laylat al-Qadr: 'Allahumma innaka 'Afuwwun tuhibbul-'afwa fa'fu 'anni' (O Allah, You are Forgiving, You love forgiveness, so forgive me).
2. Focusing on seeking Allah's complete pardon and mercy.

1. The Prophet's ﷺ increased generosity during Ramadan: he was more generous than the blowing wind when Jibril reviewed the Qur'an with him.
2. Combining Qur'anic study with abundant charity.

1. Devotion in the last ten days of Ramadan: tightening the waist belt, staying awake in prayer, and waking his family.
2. Ultimate spiritual focus and dedication at the climax of the blessed month.

1. Fasting six days of Shawwal following Ramadan is equivalent in divine reward to fasting the entire year perpetually.
2. Sustaining the momentum of spiritual discipline beyond Ramadan.

1. Fasting on the Day of 'Arafah (for non-pilgrims) expiates the sins of the preceding year and the coming year.
2. Immense magnitude of divine grace bestowed on this greatest day of the year.

1. Fasting on the Day of 'Ashura (10th of Muharram) expiates the sins of the previous year, commemorating Allah's deliverance of Prophet Musa (AS).
2. Universal prophetic continuity and gratitude for historical salvation.

1. Fasting the 9th of Muharram (Tasu'a) alongside the 10th ('Ashura) to distinguish Islamic practice.
2. Complete adherence to prophetic wisdom in voluntary fasts.

1. Fasting three days of every lunar month (the White Days: 13th, 14th, and 15th) is equivalent to a lifetime of fasting.
2. Rhythmic, lifelong commitment to regular voluntary purification.

1. The virtue of fasting Mondays and Thursdays: deeds are presented to Allah on these two days, and the Prophet ﷺ loved to have his deeds presented while fasting.
2. Weekly spiritual accounting and alignment with heavenly presentation.

1. The best voluntary fast is the fast of Prophet Dawud (AS): fasting alternate days (one day on, one day off).
2. Peak balance between worship, bodily health, and family responsibilities.

1. Severe prohibition of fasting continuously for a whole lifetime without break (Sawm al-Dahr).
2. Rejection of monastic excess; Islam promotes moderate, sustainable devotion.

1. Prohibition of fasting on the two days of Eid: Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.
2. Joyous celebration and eating with gratitude on festive Islamic days.

1. Prohibition of singling out Friday solely for voluntary fasting, or singling out its night for night prayer without regular habit.
2. Preserving the balanced nature of weekly congregational days.

1. Prohibition of fasting the Day of Doubt (Yawm al-Shakk) right before Ramadan begins, unless coinciding with a regular habitual fast.
2. Relying on verified moon sighting and maintaining certainty.

1. Fast upon sighting the new crescent moon, and break your fast upon sighting it; if clouded, complete thirty days of Sha'ban.
2. Simplicity and universality of Islamic lunar calendar verification.

1. Commencing the intention (Niyyah) for obligatory Ramadan fasting before the break of dawn (Fajr).
2. Sincerity and mental determination are essential conditions for accepted fasting.

1. Permissibility of intending voluntary fasting during the daytime before Zuhr, provided no food or drink was consumed.
2. Ease and flexibility granted in voluntary worship.

1. Permissibility of kissing and affectionate contact with one's spouse while fasting, provided one has self-control.
2. Natural human affection without violating the boundaries of fasting.

1. Severe expiation (Kaffarah) for intentional marital intercourse during the daytime of Ramadan: freeing a slave, or fasting two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people.
2. Strict sanctity of Ramadan's daylight hours.

1. Permissibility of using the toothstick (Siwak) and rinsing the mouth while fasting without swallowing water.
2. Personal hygiene is encouraged throughout the fasting day.

1. Permissibility of pouring cool water over the head or taking a bath to relieve extreme heat while fasting.
2. Physical comfort does not detract from the validity of the fast.

1. Rulings for sick and traveling individuals: concession to break fast and make up the missed days later.
2. Embracing divine concessions with ease and gratitude.

1. It is not an act of righteousness to fast during travel if it causes severe hardship and distress.
2. Protecting health and avoiding unnecessary suffering in worship.

1. Elderly people and those with chronic illnesses who cannot fast feed one needy person (Fidyah) for each day missed.
2. Compassionate alternatives ensuring everyone remains connected to the blessings.

1. Pregnant and nursing mothers who fear for their health or the health of their babies are permitted to break fast.
2. Islamic priority on the preservation of maternal and infant health.

1. Making up missed Ramadan fasts before the arrival of the next Ramadan.
2. Timely settlement of obligatory devotional debts.

1. Whoever dies with obligatory fasts remaining, their guardian (Wali) may fast on their behalf.
2. The bond of family love and settling the spiritual debts of deceased loved ones.

1. Voluntary faster is the master of their own fast: they may complete it or break it if necessary.
2. Grace and ease in non-obligatory personal devotions.

1. When invited to a meal while performing a voluntary fast, one may break the fast to honor the host or politely pray for them.
2. Prioritizing brotherhood, social harmony, and consideration.

1. Spiritual retreat in the mosque (I'tikaf) during the last ten days of Ramadan to detach from worldly distractions.
2. Complete immersion in dhikr, Qur'anic contemplation, and intimate communion with Allah.

1. The person performing I'tikaf remains inside the mosque and does not leave except for essential human necessities.
2. Safeguarding the sanctity of spiritual seclusion.

1. Women may perform I'tikaf in designated, private areas of the mosque with appropriate permission and modesty.
2. Equal opportunity for spiritual elevation for believing women.

1. Concluding Ramadan with gratitude, Takbir on the eve of Eid, and paying Zakat al-Fitr.
2. Sealing a month of worship with celebratory praise and charity.

1. The supplication of the fasting person at the moment of breaking fast is never rejected.
2. Cherishing this daily golden hour of acceptance for heartfelt prayers.
